prompt: Order the steps for a federal bill to become law:

options.text: Second chamber passes identical bill text
Standing committee reviews and reports bill
President signs the enrolled bill into law
Originating chamber approves bill on floor

explanation: A bill clears committee first, passes its originating chamber, passes the other chamber in identical form, and is signed by the President.

trap_notes.default: Lawmaking flow: committee review, first chamber vote, second chamber vote, presidential signature.

prompt: Order the standard Article V steps to amend the Constitution:

options.text: Three-fourths of states ratify the amendment
Archivist certifies amendment into Constitution
Two-thirds of both chambers approve proposal
Proposal is sent to state legislatures

explanation: Two-thirds of Congress proposes an amendment, states receive it, three-fourths ratify it, and the Archivist certifies it.

trap_notes.default: Article V path: 2/3 of Congress proposes, states receive it, 3/4 of states ratify, Archivist certifies.

prompt: Order the steps to impeach and remove a federal official:

options.text: Senate conducts trial with Chief Justice
Two-thirds Senate vote removes the official
House committee investigates alleged offenses
House majority votes articles of impeachment

explanation: The House investigates and impeaches by simple majority; the Senate then holds a trial where a two-thirds vote removes.

trap_notes.default: Impeachment sequence: House investigates, House impeaches (majority), Senate tries, Senate convicts (2/3).

prompt: Order the steps to appoint a U.S. Supreme Court justice:

options.text: Senate Judiciary Committee holds public hearings
Nominee takes judicial oath to begin service
President selects and nominates a candidate
Full Senate confirms nominee by majority vote

explanation: The President nominates a candidate, the Judiciary Committee holds hearings, the full Senate confirms, and the justice takes the oath.

trap_notes.default: Process: President nominates, Judiciary Committee holds hearings, full Senate confirms, justice takes oath.

prompt: Order how a federal lawsuit reaches the U.S. Supreme Court:

options.text: Four justices vote to grant writ of certiorari
Federal district court holds initial trial
Losing party petitions Supreme Court for review
Circuit court of appeals reviews trial record

explanation: A case starts in district court, moves to a circuit court of appeals, is petitioned to the Supreme Court, and needs four votes for cert.

trap_notes.default: Path: district court trial, circuit appeal, cert petition, Rule of Four grants review.

prompt: Order how the Supreme Court decides a case after granting review:

options.text: Justices meet in private conference to vote
Majority opinion is published as precedent
Attorneys present oral arguments to the bench
Assigned justice drafts the majority opinion

explanation: After oral arguments, the justices vote in conference, draft and circulate opinions, and publish the final ruling.

trap_notes.default: Decision flow: oral arguments, private conference vote, opinion drafting, public release.

prompt: Order how the Senate ends a filibuster using Rule XXII cloture:

options.text: Sixty senators vote to invoke cloture
Senators hold the floor to delay a bill
Senate holds final up-or-down vote on bill
Sixteen senators file a cloture petition

explanation: When senators filibuster, 16 senators file a cloture motion, 60 senators must vote to limit debate, and then a final vote occurs.

trap_notes.default: Cloture path: filibuster begins, 16 file petition, 60 vote for cloture, final bill vote.

prompt: Order how the Electoral College elects a U.S. President:

options.text: Electors meet in state capitals to cast ballots
Congress counts electoral votes in joint session
Voters cast November ballots for party slates
States certify winners and appoint electors

explanation: Voters cast ballots in November, states certify and appoint electors, electors vote in December, and Congress counts votes in January.

trap_notes.default: Sequence: November popular vote, state certification, December elector vote, January congressional count.

prompt: Order what happens if no candidate wins 270 electoral votes:

options.text: House votes by state delegation among top three
Joint session confirms no 270-vote majority
Candidate winning 26 states becomes President
Contingent election shifts to House of Representatives

explanation: Under the 12th Amendment, if no one reaches 270 electoral votes, the House votes by state delegation and 26 states elect the President.

trap_notes.default: 12th Amendment flow: no 270 majority, House takes over, one vote per state, 26 states win.

prompt: Order how a Vice Presidential vacancy is filled under the 25th Amendment:

options.text: House and Senate confirm by simple majorities
Vice Presidency becomes vacant mid-term
Confirmed nominee takes oath as Vice President
President nominates a replacement candidate

explanation: When the Vice Presidency is vacant, the President nominates a replacement who takes office after majority approval in both chambers.

trap_notes.default: 25th Amendment Section 2: vacancy occurs, President nominates, both House and Senate confirm, oath taken.

prompt: Order how a federal agency issues a binding regulation:

options.text: Agency publishes proposed rule in Federal Register
Public and stakeholders submit written comments
Congress passes law granting rulemaking power
Agency issues final rule with legal force

explanation: Congress delegates authority by statute, the agency proposes a rule, the public comments, and the agency publishes the final rule.

trap_notes.default: Rulemaking flow: statute authorizes, proposed rule published, public comments, final rule issued.

prompt: Order the sequence of a federal felony prosecution:

options.text: Grand jury reviews probable cause and indicts
Petit jury hears trial evidence and deliberates
Police arrest suspect and file initial charges
Jury returns verdict of guilty or not guilty

explanation: After arrest, a grand jury issues an indictment, a petit jury hears evidence at trial, and the jury delivers a verdict.

trap_notes.default: Criminal flow: arrest, grand jury indictment, petit jury trial, verdict.

prompt: Order how Miranda protections operate during police questioning:

options.text: Officers read right to silence and counsel
Suspect knowingly waives rights or stays silent
Police take suspect into custodial detention
Officers prepare to interrogate the suspect

explanation: Miranda applies once a suspect is in custody and about to be interrogated; officers read warnings before questioning proceeds.

trap_notes.default: Miranda trigger: custody, intent to interrogate, warnings read, suspect waives or invokes rights.

prompt: Order how the exclusionary rule enforces the Fourth Amendment:

options.text: Defense attorney files a motion to suppress
Police seize evidence without a valid warrant
Prosecution cannot use tainted items at trial
Judge rules the search violated Fourth Amendment

explanation: If police conduct an unlawful search, the defense moves to suppress, the judge finds a violation, and the evidence is barred at trial.

trap_notes.default: Exclusionary sequence: unlawful search, motion to suppress, judicial ruling, evidence excluded.

prompt: Order how selective incorporation applies Bill of Rights limits to states:

options.text: Supreme Court links right to Due Process Clause
State passes law restricting a core liberty
State law is struck down as unconstitutional
Citizen challenges law under 14th Amendment

explanation: When a state restricts a fundamental right, a challenger invokes the 14th Amendment, the Court incorporates the right, and the law falls.

trap_notes.default: Incorporation flow: state restriction, 14th Amendment challenge, Due Process linkage, state law voided.

prompt: Order how federal judicial review invalidates an unconstitutional law:

options.text: Injured party files lawsuit challenging statute
Court declares conflicting statute null and void
Congress enacts a federal statute into law
Court compares statute against constitutional text

explanation: After Congress passes a law, an injured party must sue; the court then measures it against the Constitution and voids it if it conflicts.

trap_notes.default: Judicial review requires a real lawsuit: law enacted, party sues, court compares text, law voided.

prompt: Order the decennial cycle that updates U.S. House districts:

options.text: States redraw congressional district boundaries
U.S. Census counts population every ten years
Voters elect representatives from new districts
435 House seats are reapportioned among states

explanation: First the Census counts residents, then 435 seats are reapportioned among states, states draw new maps, and elections use them.

trap_notes.default: Decennial cycle: Census count, seat reapportionment, state redistricting, congressional elections.

prompt: Order how a major U.S. party chooses its presidential nominee:

options.text: Delegates vote formally at national convention
Candidates compete in state primaries and caucuses
Party nominee campaigns for November election
States award pledged delegates to contenders

explanation: Candidates run in state primaries and caucuses to win pledged delegates, who nominate the candidate at the national convention.

trap_notes.default: Nomination flow: primaries/caucuses, delegate awards, convention vote, general election campaign.

prompt: Order the annual steps to enact federal discretionary spending:

options.text: Congress adopts an overall budget resolution
President signs enacted appropriations bills
President submits a proposed federal budget
Appropriations committees pass spending bills

explanation: The President proposes a budget, Congress sets targets in a resolution, passes appropriations bills, and the President signs them.

trap_notes.default: Budget sequence: presidential proposal, budget resolution, appropriations bills, presidential signature.

prompt: Order how a pocket veto prevents a bill from becoming law:

options.text: Congress adjourns before ten-day window ends
Bill dies without possibility of veto override
House and Senate send passed bill to President
President neither signs nor returns the bill

explanation: If Congress sends a bill and adjourns within 10 days, the President's inaction kills the bill via pocket veto with no override chance.

trap_notes.default: Pocket veto: bill sent, Congress adjourns within 10 days, President takes no action, bill dies.

prompt: Order the constitutional steps to make a U.S. treaty binding:

options.text: Two-thirds of Senate votes to give consent
President signs and exchanges treaty instruments
Executive branch negotiates terms with foreign state
President submits signed treaty to the Senate

explanation: The President negotiates a treaty, submits it to the Senate for a two-thirds vote of advice and consent, and then ratifies it.

trap_notes.default: Treaty path: negotiate, submit to Senate, 2/3 Senate consent, presidential ratification.

prompt: Order the timeline required by the 1973 War Powers Resolution:

options.text: President notifies Congress within 48 hours
Troops must withdraw absent congressional approval
President deploys U.S. forces into hostilities
Sixty-day authorization clock runs in Congress

explanation: After deploying troops, the President must notify Congress within 48 hours and withdraw within 60 days unless Congress approves.

trap_notes.default: War Powers clock: deploy forces, 48-hour notice, 60-day limit, withdrawal without approval.

prompt: Order the standard steps to become a naturalized U.S. citizen:

options.text: Applicant passes English and U.S. civics exams
Lawful permanent resident files N-400 petition
Applicant takes the Oath of Allegiance
USCIS conducts biometrics and background check

explanation: A permanent resident applies, completes biometrics and background checks, passes English and civics tests, and takes the Oath of Allegiance.

trap_notes.default: Naturalization steps: N-400 application, background check, civics/English test, Oath of Allegiance.

prompt: Order how a citizen ballot initiative becomes state law:

options.text: Election officials verify required signatures
Voters approve measure by majority on Election Day
Citizens draft text and gather voter signatures
State places the qualified initiative on ballot

explanation: Citizens draft and circulate a petition, officials verify the signatures, the measure goes on the ballot, and a majority vote enacts it.

trap_notes.default: Initiative path: gather signatures, verify signatures, place on ballot, majority voter approval.

prompt: Order how voters remove a state official through a recall election:

options.text: Special election asks voters whether to remove
Organizers collect recall petition signatures
Ousted official is replaced by chosen successor
State certifies enough valid signatures for ballot

explanation: Voters gather recall signatures, officials certify them, a special recall election is held, and a successor takes office if recalled.

trap_notes.default: Recall steps: gather signatures, certify petition, hold recall vote, seat successor.

prompt: Order how a state governor exercises a line-item veto:

options.text: Governor strikes specific spending lines only
State legislature passes an appropriations bill
Legislature may vote to override struck items
Unvetoed parts of the budget take legal effect

explanation: After lawmakers pass a budget, a governor uses the line-item veto to strike parts, the rest becomes law, and lawmakers can override.

trap_notes.default: Line-item veto: legislature passes budget, governor strikes items, remainder becomes law, override option.

prompt: Order how a no-confidence vote works in a parliamentary system:

options.text: Majority of parliament votes against government
Opposition introduces a motion of no confidence
New cabinet forms or snap election is called
Prime minister and cabinet must step down

explanation: After an opposition motion passes by majority vote, the prime minister and cabinet resign, triggering a new coalition or snap election.

trap_notes.default: Parliamentary crisis: motion introduced, majority votes no confidence, cabinet resigns, new government or election.

prompt: Order the causal chain from Shays' Rebellion to the U.S. Constitution:

options.text: Delegates meet in Philadelphia to write charter
Indebted farmers revolt in western Massachusetts
National leaders urge stronger central authority
Confederation Congress lacks funds or troops

explanation: Shays' Rebellion exposed Congress's inability to raise troops, convincing leaders to meet in Philadelphia and draft a new Constitution.

trap_notes.default: Causal chain: farmers revolt, Congress lacks power, leaders call for reform, Philadelphia convention.

prompt: Order the causal sequence in Marbury v. Madison:

options.text: Court strikes down part of Judiciary Act of 1789
Madison withholds Marbury's signed commission
Judicial review becomes binding Supreme Court power
Marbury sues directly in the Supreme Court

explanation: When Madison withheld his commission, Marbury sued under the Judiciary Act; Marshall voided that section and established judicial review.

trap_notes.default: Marbury chain: commission withheld, Marbury sues, Section 13 voided, judicial review established.

prompt: Order how Gideon v. Wainwright reshaped state criminal trials:

options.text: Supreme Court incorporates Sixth Amendment counsel
Florida judge denies Gideon a court-appointed lawyer
States must fund public defenders for poor defendants
Gideon appeals his conviction from prison

explanation: Denied a lawyer in Florida, Gideon petitioned the Supreme Court, which incorporated the Sixth Amendment and required state public defenders.

trap_notes.default: Gideon chain: lawyer denied, prison appeal, 6th Amendment incorporated, states fund public defenders.

prompt: Order the causal impact of the Voting Rights Act of 1965:

options.text: Federal examiners register disenfranchised voters
Voting Rights Act suspends discriminatory tests
More minority officials win state and local seats
Black voter registration surges across the South

explanation: The 1965 Act suspended literacy tests and sent federal examiners, causing Black registration to surge and diversifying elected offices.

trap_notes.default: VRA impact: tests suspended, federal examiners sent, registration surges, elected offices diversify.

prompt: Order how poll taxes were eliminated from all U.S. elections:

options.text: 24th Amendment bans poll taxes in federal races
Harper v. Virginia ends poll taxes in state races
Southern states adopt poll taxes to block poor voters
Financial barriers to casting ballots are removed

explanation: States used poll taxes until the 24th Amendment banned them in federal elections (1964) and Harper ended them in state elections (1966).

trap_notes.default: Poll tax end: state poll taxes adopted, 24th Amendment (federal), Harper ruling (state), barrier removed.

prompt: Order how a conference committee resolves House-Senate bill differences:

options.text: Conference committee drafts a compromise report
House and Senate pass conflicting versions of bill
President receives the unified final bill
Both chambers vote on identical compromise text

explanation: When House and Senate pass different bills, a conference committee blends them so both pass identical text for the President.

trap_notes.default: Conference path: differing bills pass, conference compromises, both pass identical text, President receives bill.

prompt: Order how a discharge petition forces a stalled House bill to the floor:

options.text: Majority of 218 House members sign petition
Standing committee chair refuses to advance bill
Full House debates and votes on the bill
Bill is discharged directly to House floor

explanation: When a committee stalls a bill, 218 House members can sign a discharge petition to pull it from committee for a full floor vote.

trap_notes.default: Discharge steps: committee stalls bill, 218 members sign, bill moves to floor, full House votes.

prompt: Order how the Supremacy Clause resolves federal-state legal conflicts:

options.text: Court applies Article VI Supremacy Clause
State enacts statute that conflicts with U.S. law
Congress passes valid law under Article I
Valid federal law preempts the state statute

explanation: When a state law conflicts with a valid federal statute, courts apply the Supremacy Clause and federal law preempts the state law.

trap_notes.default: Preemption flow: valid federal law, conflicting state law, Supremacy Clause applied, state law preempted.

prompt: Order how conditional federal grants shape state laws:

options.text: State raises drinking age to keep full funding
Congress ties highway grants to drinking-age rule
Federal government disburses full highway aid
Supreme Court upholds grant condition as valid

explanation: Congress tied highway funds to a 21 drinking age, the Court upheld the condition in South Dakota v. Dole, and states complied to keep funds.

trap_notes.default: Fiscal federalism: Congress attaches condition, Court upholds power, state complies, federal funds flow.

prompt: Order how partisan gerrymandering reduces election competition:

options.text: Mapmakers pack or crack rival party voters
General elections become less competitive
One party controls state redistricting process
Districts produce predictable safe partisan seats

explanation: A controlling party packs or cracks opponents when drawing maps, creating safe seats that make general elections less competitive.

trap_notes.default: Gerrymander chain: party controls map, packs/cracks rivals, safe seats form, competition drops.

prompt: Order how an independent regulatory commission enforces federal standards:

options.text: Commission investigates alleged rule violations
Congress establishes independent regulatory board
Commission imposes civil fines or cease orders
Board issues safety or market compliance rules

explanation: Congress creates an independent commission, which writes industry rules, investigates violations, and issues penalties.

trap_notes.default: Regulatory cycle: Congress creates board, board writes rules, investigates breaches, imposes penalties.

prompt: Order how a citizen obtains records under the Freedom of Information Act:

options.text: Agency searches files for responsive records
Requester receives non-exempt public documents
Citizen or journalist submits written FOIA request
Agency redacts classified or private exemptions

explanation: A requester files a FOIA request, the agency locates responsive records, redacts statutory exemptions, and releases the rest.

trap_notes.default: FOIA process: request filed, records searched, exemptions redacted, documents released.

prompt: Order how a writ of habeas corpus challenges unlawful detention:

options.text: Jailer must bring detainee and show legal cause
Judge orders release if detention lacks lawful basis
Detained person petitions a court for a writ
Government holds an individual in custody

explanation: A detained person petitions for habeas corpus, forcing officials to justify custody in court or release the prisoner.

trap_notes.default: Habeas flow: person detained, writ petitioned, jailer justifies custody, judge orders release if unlawful.

prompt: Order the causal chain from the 1800 election to the 12th Amendment:

options.text: House breaks deadlock after 36 ballots
12th Amendment separates presidential and VP votes
Jefferson and Burr tie in electoral votes
Congress proposes reform to prevent ticket ties

explanation: The 1800 tie between Jefferson and Burr forced 36 House ballots, prompting the nation to adopt separate ballots via the 12th Amendment.

trap_notes.default: 1800 crisis: Jefferson-Burr tie, 36 House ballots, reform proposed, 12th Amendment ratified.

prompt: Order how the Great Compromise broke the 1787 convention deadlock:

options.text: Connecticut delegates propose two-house Congress
Large and small states clash over representation
Convention adopts House by population, equal Senate
Virginia and New Jersey Plans stall in debate

explanation: Clashes between the Virginia and New Jersey Plans led Connecticut delegates to propose a bicameral compromise that the convention adopted.

trap_notes.default: 1787 sequence: state clash, rival plans stall, Connecticut proposal, bicameral Congress adopted.

prompt: Order how a presidential veto threat shapes a bill before passage:

options.text: Lawmakers revise contested provisions in bill
White House signals opposition to draft bill
President signs the compromised legislation
Bill advances in congressional committee

explanation: When a bill advances, a presidential veto threat pushes lawmakers to modify contested clauses so the final bill earns a signature.

trap_notes.default: Bargaining flow: bill advances, veto threat issued, bill amended, President signs compromise.

prompt: Order how a city gains local self-governance under a home-rule charter:

options.text: Local voters adopt a municipal home-rule charter
City council passes local zoning and ordinances
State constitution authorizes municipal home rule
City manages local services without state bills

explanation: Once a state authorizes home rule, local voters adopt a charter, empowering the city council to pass ordinances and run local services.

trap_notes.default: Home rule chain: state authorization, voter-adopted charter, local ordinances, self-managed services.

geo.label: U.S. Department of State, Washington, D.C.

prompt: Order how economic sanctions operate as a nonmilitary foreign policy tool:

options.text: Target country faces trade and currency strain
U.S. freezes assets and restricts trade ties
Target regime violates international norms
Target enters talks to ease economic pressure

explanation: After a regime violates norms, sanctions freeze assets and trade, creating economic strain that pressures the target to negotiate.

trap_notes.default: Sanctions chain: norm violation, asset/trade freeze, economic strain, diplomatic talks.

items.text: Only registered party members may vote
Prevents rival-party crossover voting
Any registered voter chooses a party ballot
Allows independent voters to participate

prompt: Sort each primary rule into Closed Primary or Open Primary.
explanation: Closed primaries restrict voting to registered party members; open primaries let any registered voter pick a party ballot.

trap_notes.default: Closed primaries require prior party registration; open primaries let independents and others choose a ballot.

items.text: Restricted to narrow, specific projects
Include strict federal spending rules
Support broad policy areas like health
Give states wide spending discretion

prompt: Sort each federal grant feature into Categorical Grants or Block Grants.
explanation: Categorical grants fund specific purposes with strict rules; block grants give states broad discretion within wide policy areas.

trap_notes.default: Categorical grants have narrow rules; block grants give states broad flexibility.

items.text: Hold jury trials and hear witnesses
Presided over by a single trial judge
Hear cases in three-judge panels
Review trial records for legal errors

prompt: Sort each federal court trait into U.S. District Courts or U.S. Courts of Appeals.
explanation: District courts are single-judge trial courts with juries; circuit courts of appeals sit in three-judge panels to review legal errors.

trap_notes.default: District courts hold trials with juries; appellate courts use three-judge panels to review records.

items.text: Favors broader social safety-net programs
Backs active federal market regulation
Favors lower taxes and deregulation
Emphasizes traditional social institutions

prompt: Sort each policy stance into Modern American Liberalism or Conservatism.
explanation: Modern liberalism favors active federal regulation and social programs; conservatism favors lower taxes, deregulation, and tradition.

trap_notes.default: Liberalism backs regulation and social programs; conservatism backs lower taxes and traditional institutions.

items.text: Single top candidate wins entire district
Tends to reinforce a two-party system
Seats match each party's vote share
Encourages multiparty coalition cabinets

prompt: Sort each electoral trait into Winner-Take-All Districts or Proportional Representation.
explanation: Winner-take-all districts favor two major parties; proportional representation awards seats by vote share and fosters coalitions.

trap_notes.default: Winner-take-all favors two parties; proportional representation mirrors vote share and aids smaller parties.

items.text: Votes strictly as constituents prefer
Mirrors district opinion polls closely
Uses personal judgment on complex bills
May vote against short-term local opinion

prompt: Sort each legislative behavior into Delegate Model or Trustee Model.
explanation: A delegate follows constituents' direct wishes; a trustee relies on independent judgment for the broader public good.

trap_notes.default: Delegates mirror voter wishes; trustees rely on their own judgment.

items.text: Orders a lower court to send case records
Granted when four justices agree
Orders a jailer to justify holding a prisoner
Protected in Article I against suspension

prompt: Sort each legal feature into Writ of Certiorari or Writ of Habeas Corpus.
explanation: Certiorari brings a lower-court case up for Supreme Court review; habeas corpus challenges unlawful physical detention.

trap_notes.default: Certiorari calls up appellate records; habeas corpus challenges unlawful detention.

items.text: Bars creating an official church
Forbids state-authored public school prayer
Protects individuals' right to worship freely
Shields sincere religious practice from bans

prompt: Sort each protection into Establishment Clause or Free Exercise Clause.
explanation: The Establishment Clause stops government from endorsing religion; the Free Exercise Clause protects individuals' religious practice.

trap_notes.default: Establishment bars state-sponsored religion; Free Exercise protects personal worship and practice.

items.text: Divides spheres like a layer cake
Prevailed across most of the 19th century
Blends roles like a marble cake
Expanded rapidly during the 1930s New Deal

prompt: Sort each federalism trait into Dual Federalism or Cooperative Federalism.
explanation: Dual federalism kept federal and state spheres separate; cooperative federalism blended them through shared programs since the New Deal.

trap_notes.default: Dual = layer cake (19th century); Cooperative = marble cake (New Deal onward).

items.text: Sets strict time limits on floor debate
Decides whether floor amendments are allowed
Allows minority senators to extend debate
Requires 60 votes under Rule XXII to end

prompt: Sort each legislative mechanism into House Rules Committee or Senate Filibuster.
explanation: The House Rules Committee controls debate time and amendments; the Senate filibuster lets senators extend debate unless 60 invoke cloture.

trap_notes.default: House Rules Committee limits debate; Senate filibuster extends debate until 60-vote cloture.

items.text: Subject to strict per-election dollar caps
Paid directly to a candidate's campaign
May raise unlimited sums from corporations
Cannot coordinate ads with a candidate

prompt: Sort each rule into Direct Candidate Contributions or Super PAC Spending.
explanation: Direct campaign donations face strict FEC dollar limits; Super PACs raise unlimited sums but must act independently of candidates.

trap_notes.default: Direct donations are capped by law; Super PACs are unlimited but barred from coordinating.

items.text: Requires two-thirds Senate consent
Explicitly outlined in Article II text
Signed by President without Senate vote
Can be reversed by a later President

prompt: Sort each foreign-policy pact into Formal Treaty or Executive Agreement.
explanation: Article II treaties require two-thirds Senate approval; executive agreements are presidential pacts that do not need Senate consent.

trap_notes.default: Treaties need 2/3 of the Senate; executive agreements do not and can be undone by a future President.

items.text: Elected mayor serves as chief executive
Separates executive and council powers
City council hires a professional manager
Appointed administrator runs daily services

prompt: Sort each city-government feature into Mayor-Council or Council-Manager System.
explanation: Mayor-council cities elect a chief executive mayor; council-manager cities hire a professional city manager to run operations.

trap_notes.default: Mayor-council uses an elected executive mayor; council-manager hires a professional administrator.

items.text: Candidate with the most votes wins outright
Winner can take office under 50 percent
Requires winning more than half of votes
Holds a second round if no one hits 50%

prompt: Sort each election rule into Plurality Voting or Majority Runoff Voting.
explanation: Plurality elections award victory to the highest vote-getter even under 50%; majority runoff systems require over 50% of votes.

trap_notes.default: Plurality = most votes wins; Majority runoff = over 50% required, or top two face a runoff.

items.text: Readily strikes down elected-branch laws
Willingly overturns older court precedents
Defers heavily to legislative policy choices
Adheres closely to stare decisis precedent

prompt: Sort each judicial approach into Judicial Activism or Judicial Restraint.
explanation: Judicial activism is willing to void laws and precedent to protect rights; judicial restraint defers to lawmakers and precedent.

trap_notes.default: Activism voids laws and precedents more readily; restraint defers to legislatures and stare decisis.
